content.title: Identifying the Control Group and Its Purpose
content.overview: In ACT Science, identifying the control group is essential for understanding experimental design. The control group serves as the baseline for comparison, allowing researchers to determine if the experimental treatment actually caused the observed effects.
learning_objectives: Define the control group in a scientific experiment.
Identify the control group based on descriptions of 'no treatment' or 'standard conditions'.
Explain the purpose of a control group as a baseline for comparison.
Verify that controlled variables remain constant across all groups to ensure a valid comparison.

sections.title: Defining the Control Group
sections.content: The control group is the group in an experiment that does not receive the experimental treatment or is kept under standard, 'normal' conditions. While the experimental groups are subjected to changes (the independent variable), the control group provides a point of reference. By comparing the results of the experimental groups to the control group, scientists can see the magnitude of the effect caused by the treatment.

sections.title: The Baseline-Check Strategy
sections.content:
To identify the control group on the ACT, look for the group described as receiving 'no treatment,' 'zero concentration,' or the 'standard condition.' Once identified, confirm that all other variables—such as light, water, temperature, and duration—are identical across all groups. This ensures that any difference in the dependent variable (the outcome) is due solely to the experimental treatment and not an outside factor.

![A flowchart showing the steps to identify a control group: Locate 'No Treatment' group, Confirm constant variables, and Establish baseline.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/a9134431-b184-4396-810e-882778e43b84-1786506667150-707.webp)

sections.title: The Purpose of the Control
sections.content: The primary purpose of a control group is to serve as a baseline. Without a control, you cannot know if the results would have happened anyway. For example, if plants grow 10 inches with a new fertilizer, you don't know if the fertilizer worked unless you have a control group (no fertilizer) that grew only 5 inches. The control allows you to attribute the 5-inch difference specifically to the fertilizer.

worked_examples.question: Researchers test two fertilizers on lettuce over 4 weeks. All plants receive 12 hours of light, 200 mL of water daily, and use the same soil. Group A receives no fertilizer. Group B receives Fertilizer X (a standard brand). Group C receives Fertilizer Y (a new formula). The average final mass is: A=45g, B=60g, C=55g. Which group is the control and why?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Locate the group with no special treatment. Group A is explicitly listed as receiving no fertilizer. Step 2: Confirm other variables. Light, water, and soil are identical across all groups, meaning the fertilizer is the only difference. Step 3: State the purpose. Group A provides the baseline mass of 45g. By comparing B (60g) and C (55g) to A (45g), we can conclude that both fertilizers increased mass, but Fertilizer X was more effective. Therefore, Group A is the control.

common_mistakes: Mistaking a 'standard treatment' for a true control: While a standard brand (like Fertilizer X) is a point of comparison, the true control is the group with no treatment at all (Group A).
Assuming every experiment has a control: While most ACT experiments do, always look for the specific 'no treatment' or 'baseline' label rather than guessing.

Confusing controlled variables with the control group: Controlled variables are factors kept the same (like temperature), whereas the control group is the specific set of subjects receiving no treatment.
exam_tips: Look for the value '0' in data tables; this often indicates the control group (e.g., 0 mg of a drug).
If a question asks for the 'purpose' of a specific group that received no treatment, the answer almost always involves the word 'baseline' or 'comparison'.
Check that all groups were treated identically except for the one variable being tested.
content.recap: The control group is the 'no-treatment' or 'standard' group that serves as a baseline. It allows researchers to isolate the effects of the independent variable by providing a reference point for comparison.

knowledge_claims.content: The control group is the group in an experiment that receives no experimental treatment or is maintained under standard conditions.
The primary purpose of a control group is to provide a baseline for comparison to evaluate the effects of the experimental treatment.
A control group can often be identified in a data table by a treatment level of zero or a label such as 'standard' or 'none'.
To ensure a valid comparison, all variables except the experimental treatment (such as light, water, and temperature) must be identical between the control and experimental groups.
Differences in outcomes between the experimental group and the control group are attributed to the independent variable being tested.
It is a mistake to label a group receiving a 'standard' treatment as the control if there is another group receiving 'no' treatment at all.
Unlike experimental groups which test new conditions, the control group represents the 'normal' or 'untreated' state of the system.
When analyzing an ACT Science passage, the first step in identifying the control is locating the group that lacks the specific variable being investigated.
A valid experiment requires that the control group be subjected to the same environmental constants as the experimental groups.
If a control group and an experimental group show the same results, the experimental treatment likely had no effect.
Standard conditions refer to the typical environment or procedure used as a reference point when a 'no treatment' group is not possible.
The control group helps researchers rule out external factors, such as time or natural growth, as the cause of observed changes.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 2: Dissolving Effervescent Tablets
Students tested how water temperature affects the time required for identical effervescent tablets to stop producing visible bubbles. In Experiment 1, they used 200 mL of water at four temperatures and one whole tablet per trial. In Experiment 2, they repeated the test with crushed tablets while keeping the water volume and temperatures unchanged.

Which choice correctly identifies the independent variable(s) in the investigation?

options.D: the numerical labels printed on the graph

items.explanation: Independent variables are intentionally varied or used to define treatment conditions.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 5: Protective Coatings and Corrosion
Steel washers were cleaned, weighed, and coated with no coating, wax, paint, or a plant-based film. The washers were placed in equal volumes of saltwater for 10 days, dried, and reweighed. Greater mass loss indicates more corrosion. A second observation recorded the percentage of each surface covered by rust.

Which choice correctly identifies the independent variable(s) in the investigation?

options.B: washer type, saltwater volume, and exposure time
options.C: the numerical labels printed on the graph

items.explanation: Independent variables are intentionally varied or used to define treatment conditions.
